meta.title: Do you let LLMs write both your tests and your code?
meta.author: travisgriggs
meta.body:
I'm curious what stance others have taken? Or what they've experienced with this? I'm toying with adding a rule to our values.md that the LLM can only significantly generate one or the other.

I'm reviewing a merge request at the moment where it's clear the LLM mostly did both, and they're highly tautological. And I can see how it over engineered the code, just to be able to write more tests almost.

comments.author: motet-a
comments.text:
I really dislike this as well, and I’m not a supporter of LLMs, but some humans can also do this without any LLM. Maybe you can simply say that it’s over-engineered and that the tests are bad. I think it’s a valid reason to refuse to merge a PR.

But to answer your question, I have used LLMs to write both tests and code a few times…

comments.author: nesk
comments.text:
I went from your stance to another one: you can generate both with LLMs, but you have to prove that the tests are properly testing your code. This can be done by surgically breaking the implementation for each assertion and check if the test properly fails.

Since it takes a lot of time to do by hand, I'm working on a skill to ease the process.

Another thing that could help is mutation testing.

comments.author: LolPython
comments.text:
This can be done by surgically breaking the implementation for each assertion and check if the test properly fails.


No harm in making a skill but I have had some success getting LLMs to do that by asking it to do manual mutation testing

comments.author: gf0
comments.text: I think simply asking it to do red-green testing will catch most bad generated tests.

comments.author: fedemp
comments.text:
This can be done by surgically breaking the implementation for each assertion and check if the test properly fails


The agent we use at work loves to do that by itself whenever I ask it to create tests for the new feature it created.

comments.author: joshka
comments.text:
Yes. Tests are just code which should be heavily constrained to be:


simple

short

linear

WET not DRY

deterministic

explanatory rather than algorithmic

non tautological

descriptive of the failure mode (i.e. don't assert(foo.is_empty) instead assert_eq(foo, []))

covering the useful branches of the implementation

usually correct (exception: characterization tests used to note drift prior to fixing a bug)


The tests that come out of the default models sometimes tend to not quite fit this, but most frontier models respond pretty well to steering to get this right, so invest in a good set of rules that match your domain on this. There's lots of simple rules you can build up to write better tests in any language.

The thing about tests and LLMs is that you can use just two of the things spec + impl or spec + test in isolation and have the model reason over them for whether they're correct. This is a sort of triangulation type thing that you do as a developer and it's reasonable to do with an LLM too and not just treat it like a black box that summons code into being in one incantation.

The other thing you can do is have the LLM quickly go through the process of testing the Red/Green steps in TDD (whether pre-testing or post-testing) to ensure that a failure shows up somehow and is correctly indicating what went wrong.

LLMs are better at this than humans, assuming they get decent inputs upfront.

comments.author: kqr
comments.text:
I do have LLMs generate both implementation and tests. But I spend a lot of time thinking about what needs to be tested and how, to give me confidence the implementation is correct. I.e. I don't give the LLM free reign in deciding what and how to test.

I'm actively experimenting with methods for getting verification right at a pace faster than I can personally guarantee all of the implementation. Things like STAMP/STPA, mutation testing, fuzzing etc. that aim to make verification sliyghtly more algorithmic could be fruitful ways forward. But it's still early days and I have to step in and manually correct a lot.

comments.author: gerardnico
comments.text:
That’s the core of software engineering, now.

Steering the model to generate professional grade code and not over generating for the sake of generating.

In all my task, I describe a goal which is a test that obviously it writes. Even with natural language, its code after all.

I tend to refactor myself because writing the prompt that a llm would understand take for me now more times that using the ide facilities. Need to work on that.

comments.author: cr8
comments.text:
To me a lot of LLM tests feel like "scaffolding" - they are not written like you would write a test you intend to keep, but may have helped it validate something that does not need to continually be validated once the code is done.

As such, I have arranged things such that most of the tests it writes wind up in a directory that is, by default, gitignored, and it requires more justification to put them where they'll be checked in.

comments.author: tomleo
comments.text: Sometimes code & unit tests, then I write the integration & e2e tests. It depends on the code & domain.

comments.author: kornel
comments.text:
You can't do both in a single session, because LLMs will write weaksauce tests to make its code look good.

It works better if you start a new session and give it a goal to find bugs in the code and prove that via tests.

comments.author: freddyb
comments.text: For throw-away code (HTML dashboards, code that generates graphs for slides, etc.) I don't bother looking at the code at all. The LLM writes tests and I presume it's useful to avoid regressions, but again - I don't really look.

comments.author: koreth
comments.text:
I used to be pretty opposed to this, but the models have gotten significantly better and nowadays I probably let the LLMs write both the code and the tests about half the time. The LLMs all do seem to go a bit hog-wild with low-value tests, especially "prove that the code no longer works the way it used to" tests, but (and this is the big change in recent models) you can successfully instruct them to not do that.

Using something like the Superpowers plugin helps a lot since it makes the models use a TDD-style workflow and gets them to be more rigorous about gathering requirements before even starting in on the code design.

A common flow for me is to have an initial back-and-forth to define the problem and account for all the corner cases the tool can dig up, then review its high-level design document, then let it rip on both the code and tests, and finally, tell it to go trim down and consolidate its tests. On a change I'm working on now, that last step caused my LLM to get rid of a solid 40% of its original test code without losing much utility.

Another important thing I do is review the code and the tests myself before anyone else on my team looks at them. If there are low-value or overly-verbose tests, I clean them up (usually by hand, sometimes by LLM) before sending the change out for code review.

comments.author: maduggan
comments.text: I write my own tests because otherwise I don't understand the problem and cannot judge whether the LLM produced anything of value.

comments.author: miah
comments.text: I'm still in the "haven't used LLM's to generate any code" camp. The most I've used a LLM for was to generate a backstory for a D&D character. I avoid that plague as much as I can.

comments.author: LolPython
comments.text:
It’s situational. For testing math stuff or CRUD or just making a regression test that’s representative of the bug being fixed, LLM making the code and the test has seemed to work OK especially after doing the LLM meta optimization dance (mutation testing, adversarial review). And we still make decisions around preventing code bloat like if the mocks get excessive not accepting those tests or at least having a conversation about it.

For any tests doing something really useful we’ve made those system tests or dockerized integration tests in a multi service environment pointed at a simulator and due to the business context those have usually been driven by humans either prompting for specific cases or handing off a test plan.

I could see even more delegation becoming possible (having the AI drive integration test case generation) as we are feeding even more context to the LLM as in emails, docs etc. Already we’re finding the LLM output improving a lot when we give this extra context. That flows down to even more useful tests getting generated.

Scary times!

comments.author: noteflakes
comments.text:
The other day I reviewed a PR for one of my projects that was vibe-coded. The PR comprised a single commit with a small fix and lots of additional tests. The single commit means there's no (easy) way to really make sure all those new tests would fail without the fix.

I think it would have been better to have the agent first write failing tests, commit that, then work on the fix and commit it separately. While I don't vibe-code myself, I think following a strict TDD methodology can make a big difference in this respect.

comments.author: joshka
comments.text: Typing this comment plus a link to that pr into any coding agent hooked up to any LLM from the past couple of years would have gotten you the desired effect. ;P

comments.author: mxey
comments.text:
I think it would have been better to have the agent first write failing tests, commit that, then work on the fix and commit it separately.


I wouldn’t want to commit a failing test. What I have adopted from the CUE people is writing a test that asserts the broken state and then change it in the second commit.

comments.author: reivilibre
comments.text:
I'm pretty sure I've heard of frameworks where you can annotate tests in a way that marks them as expected to fail, such that you'll get an error if they don't fail, that might also fit this idea. Can't remember where I saw this though.

https://doc.rust-lang.org/rust-by-example/testing/unit_testing.html#testing-panics #[should_panic] is the best I'm seeing for Rust

I typically just commit failing tests since we squash merge at work and so I'm not putting anyone at risk of bisecting in the middle.

comments.author: LolPython
comments.text:
Small note - pytest has @pytest.mark.xfail, i.e.:

@pytest.mark.xfail(reason="This feature is not implemented yet")

comments.author: mxey
comments.text:
I typically just commit failing tests since we squash merge at work and so I'm not putting anyone at risk of bisecting in the middle.


But does CI run for every commit before the squash? I think the point of a separate commit can be to make it clear to a code reviewer that a test indeed works.

comments.author: reivilibre
comments.text:
No, at least not unless you pushed them one at a time. (Typical GitHub behaviour, as far as I know)

I keep the delineation purely for my own sanity / the reviewer's benefit, I guess. I do revert my non-test commits and check the tests fail.
I guess I feel it as an extension of the TDD-style 'Make sure you see your test fail'. To be fair, I don't think they need to be in separate commits for that to be possible, as you could just revert the non-test files from the commit more or less as easily.
